title: CVX vs. SHEL: Which Energy Giant Offers Better Shareholder Returns? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron CorporationCVX and Shell plc SHEL continue to prioritize shareholder rewards through dividends and share repurchases, supported by strong cash generation and disciplined capital allocation. Both energy giants reported robust third-quarter 2026 results despite volatile commodity prices and geopolitical uncertainties. Chevron returned approximately $6 billion to its shareholders during the quarter, while Shell distributed $5.3 billion and announced a fresh $5 billion share repurchase program. However, their contrasting dividend policies, buyback strategies and earnings outlooks raise an important question: Which energy major offers better shareholder returns? Let's examine their fundamentals, stock performance and earnings expectations to determine which company holds the edge. Chevron has demonstrated stronger share-price momentum than Shell over the past year. CVX’s shares gained 39.1%, outperforming SHEL's 27.8% increase by 11.3 percentage points. Both stocks experienced considerable volatility during the period, particularly around midyear, before recovering in subsequent months. Chevron maintained its performance advantage despite fluctuations in energy markets. Chevron's shareholder-friendly capital allocation strategy remains a key investment attraction. During the third quarter, the company paid approximately $3.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $2.5 billion of shares. Chevron declared a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share, supported by 39 consecutive years of annual dividend increases. Management continues prioritizing dividend growth, efficient capital investments and balance-sheet strength. Shell also maintained substantial shareholder distributions, paying approximately $2.2 billion in dividends and repurchasing $3.2 billion of shares during the quarter. The company declared a quarterly dividend of 39.06 cents per ordinary share, compared with 35.80 cents in the year-ago period. Chevron's established dividend growth record offers greater visibility for income-oriented investors. Shell's higher allocation toward repurchases, meanwhile, reflects a more buyback-focused shareholder return strategy. Overall, Chevron holds the advantage in dividend consistency, while Shell demonstrates stronger near-term repurchase momentum. Shell's share repurchase strategy remains a major differentiator in its capital allocation approach. Following approximately $3.2 billion in third-quarter buybacks, Shell announced a new $5 billion repurchase program, expected to conclude by its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings announcement. The initiative reflects management's confidence in the company's cash-generating capabilities and commitment to returning surplus capital to its shareholders. Chevron, meanwhile, maintained quarterly repurchases of approximately $2.5 billion. Management reiterated its intended quarterly buyback range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. Shell's larger newly announced program provides greater near-term buyback potential, while Chevron's established framework supports distribution predictability. However, the ultimate benefits of repurchases depend on execution and the valuations at which shares are acquired. Strong cash generation remains essential for sustaining shareholder rewards through fluctuating commodity-price environments. Chevron generated $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow during third-quarter 2026. Adjusted earnings totaled $10.4 billion, supported by improved refining margins and operational efficiency. Shell generated approximately $21 billion in operating cash flow, $16.3 billion in free cash flow and $10.8 billion in adjusted earnings. Shell's stronger absolute cash generation provides considerable flexibility to finance shareholder distributions and future investments. However, the companies use different free cash flow definitions, limiting direct comparability. Chevron's net debt-to-operating-cash-flow ratio stood at 0.4 times, reflecting a robust financial position. Meanwhile, Shell's gearing improved to 16.6% from 18.7% sequentially, demonstrating strengthening balance-sheet flexibility. Both companies appear financially positioned to sustain shareholder distributions, although weaker commodity prices and elevated capital requirements could affect future cash flows. Positive earnings estimate revisions provide additional insights into the companies' profitability outlooks. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Chevron's 2026 earnings increased 13.26%, from $16.52 to $18.71 per share. Its 2027 estimate climbed 22.49%, from $14.67 to $17.97 per share. For Shell, the consensus estimate for 2026 earnings increased 15.52%, from $10.89 to $12.58 per share. Meanwhile, its 2027 estimate rose 12.14%, from $10.13 to $11.36 per share. Shell demonstrated stronger upward revisions for 2026, while Chevron recorded greater improvement in 2027 expectations. This suggests comparatively stronger longer-term earnings revision momentum for Chevron. Both Chevron and Shell offer attractive shareholder return opportunities. Shell stands out for stronger absolute cash generation and aggressive share repurchases, while Chevron benefits from consistent dividend growth, superior historical share-price performance and improving longer-term earnings expectations. Chevron's 39.1% share-price gain, 39-year dividend growth streak, robust balance sheet and stronger 2027 earnings estimate revisions collectively reinforce its investment appeal. Although both stocks carry a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), Chevron emerges as the better pick for investors prioritizing consistent shareholder returns and longer-term earnings momentum. Shell remains an appealing alternative for investors emphasizing buybacks and cash generation. Nevertheless, Chevron's dividend dependability and stronger 2027 estimate revisions give it the edge in this face-off, subject to valuation considerations. title: Chevron vs. Occidental Petroleum: Which Energy Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron maintains a diversified global footprint with operations spanning crude oil production, refining, and chemical manufacturing. Occidental Petroleum focuses on high-production basins and is aggressively expanding its carbon management and low-carbon technology capabilities. Which energy heavyweight offers the best path for your portfolio through 2027? The energy landscape is evolving as traditional oil producers balance output with shifting climate policies. Investors deciding between Chevron(NYSE:CVX)and Occidental Petroleum(NYSE:OXY)must choose between a diversified giant and a specialized producer. Chevron provides a traditional integrated model, controlling everything from extraction to retail fuel sales. Occidental Petroleum focuses on efficiency in specific North American basins while investing in emerging carbon capture technologies. This comparison explores which strategy is better positioned for the next few years. Chevron operates as a global energy leader, producing crude oil and natural gas and refining them into fuels and lubricants sold under brands such as Texaco and Caltex. The company manages a massive supply chain through partnerships such as Chevron Phillips Chemical Company and maintains an interest in Hess Midstream(NYSE:HESM). Its international commitments include nearly 3.2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas primarily from assets in Australia and Israel. In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $225.8 billion, representing a growth rate of roughly 20.8% compared to the prior period. During this time, the company reported a net income of nearly $27.0 billion. These figures highlight the scale of its global operations, though its 11.9% net margin indicates the high costs of maintaining such a broad, integrated network. Chevron (CVX) stock offers a free cash flow yield of 8.4% over the past twelve months, against 4.5% for the median S&P 500 company. A yield that high means one of two things: a business on sale, or a business the market expects to shrink. So what is that cash worth to you as an owner? As a shareholder, you own a slice of the free cash Chevron produces, whether the company pays it out or keeps it. Free cash is what is left after Chevron pays to run the business and covers its capital spending. Cash kept in the company still belongs to you. When buyers come to see that cash, the price tends to follow, and more so when the cash is growing. Chevron pumps oil and gas and refines it into fuel. Its operations brought in $52.0 billion of cash over the twelve months to September 30, 2026. Capital spending took $17.9 billion of that. That left $34.1 billion of free cash flow, more than double the $15.4 billion of a year earlier. Chevron’s free cash flow more than doubled in a year, to $34.1 billion. For most of the past three years, the cash was smaller and steadier. In every twelve-month period ending between September 2023 and March 2026, free cash flow stayed between $13.6 billion and $20.4 billion. Then the June and September quarters of 2026 brought in $30.1 billion together. The March quarter before them used more cash than it made. Chevron owed $33.5 billion on September 30, 2026, against $12.8 billion of cash and short-term investments. Its operating income covered its interest bill 24.2 times over the past twelve months. Management said Chevron cut its debt by more than $3 billion in the September quarter. The reported figures show a business growing, not shrinking. Chevron’s revenue rose 20.8% over the past twelve months. That followed two years of decline, by 4.2% and then 3.6%. Its operating margin reached 14.6%, against 8.1% a year earlier. On those results, Chevron looks more like a business on sale. Yet one reading of the high yield is that the 2026 cash came from a price spike that will pass. Oil swung between $68 and $132 a barrel in the September quarter alone, management said on its October 30, 2026 call. On management’s adjusted figures, downstream earnings rose from the June quarter, mainly on higher refining margins and volumes. Earnings from oil and gas production fell from the June quarter. The average prices Chevron realized were lower, it sold less oil and gas, and timing effects hurt. Management expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term. It pointed to 10% of the world’s refining capacity sitting offline, with exports reduced due to conflicts. The worry is that the cash may shrink once fuel flows normally again. Chevron is also adding oil of its own, so not all of its cash rests on price. It plans to double production from its three joint ventures in Venezuela to roughly 600,000 barrels a day by 2031. Management says that program will pay for itself. Chevron’s cash has already eased from its peak. Free cash flow was $12.0 billion in the September quarter, down from $18.1 billion in June. Management said sharp price increases late in the quarter hurt working capital, the cash tied up in day-to-day operations. It expects that effect to unwind when prices fall. Chevron is also increasing its exploration spending by 50% relative to 2025. Its debt is already low. By management’s measure, net debt was 0.4 times cash flow from operations at the end of September. Chevron is expected to report in January 2027. That report will show the December quarter’s free cash flow beside the two strong quarters before it, and how much Chevron owes at year-end. If that cash stays near the June and September quarters, the 8.4% yield points to a business on sale. If it falls back, the market’s doubt looks right. title: How Stronger Cash Flow At Chevron (CVX) Has Changed Its Investment Story - Simply Wall St
content:
To own Chevron, an investor needs to be comfortable with a large hydrocarbon producer that relies on low cost barrels, cost efficiencies and disciplined project spending to keep free cash flow robust enough to cover and grow dividends. The analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St assumes that execution in areas like Venezuela, the Permian and long term power contracts offsets forecast earnings and revenue declines. The latest jump in free cash flow and the reaffirmed dividend priority make near term cash returns look well supported, so they reinforce rather than change that storyline. The more immediate swing factor still appears to be refining margins and commodity prices, while the biggest risk remains faster shifts in energy demand away from hydrocarbons than Chevron’s portfolio can currently absorb. The recent update around roughly doubling Venezuela production capacity over time is one of the most relevant announcements for this narrative. Management has already committed about US$7b to a growth phase in those joint ventures, with current fiscal terms reported as immediately positive for free cash flow. That fits with the focus on capital efficient expansion instead of only new megaprojects. For you as a shareholder, Venezuela sits alongside the southern Ionian Sea exploration as a tangible test of Chevron’s ability to add resilient, low cost barrels without overstretching the balance sheet. Success would support dividend coverage and help counter the earnings declines analysts forecast. Execution setbacks, political disruption or higher long term decarbonisation pressure could weaken that role and weigh on the operating outlook. Analysts currently frame Chevron's outlook around revenues of US$218.7b and earnings of US$25.4b by 2029, based on an assumed 1.1% yearly decline in revenue and an earnings decrease of US$1.6b from current earnings of US$27.0b.
